This is typically done using alpha blending in back-to-front or front-to-back order to handle transparency correctly [S1][S2, unofficial].

The claim states that the process is typically done using alpha blending in back-to-front order. Source [S1] explicitly confirms this in the 'Splat Composition' section, stating: 'The sorting is based on the distance between the camera position and the splat's mean vector in the global space. Sorting order is back-to-front based on this depth value... Once sorted, the final color of each pixel is computed by alpha blending the splats in the sorted order.' Source [S2] discusses alternative composition methods (splat-every-sample vs slice-by-slice) but does not contradict the standard back-to-front alpha blending method described in [S1]; it merely compares performance and visual quality of different implementation strategies. Therefore, the core facts of the claim are fully supported by Source [S1].

All specific claims in the prompt are directly supported by the text in Section 3.5 and the associated equations.

The mathematical formulas provided ($ eta_i = 1 - exp(-delta_i sum sigma_{i,n})$ and $c_i = sum phi_N(sigma_{i,n}) c_{i,n}$) confirm this mechanism. 5. **Hardware Acceleration:** Most methods in this family rely on GPU rasterization pipelines for performance, enabling real-time interactivity [S1][S2, unofficial].

The claim states that 'Most methods in this family rely on GPU rasterization pipelines for performance, enabling real-time interactivity.' While Source [S1] mentions that 'transmittance is usually handled by the GPU's blending hardware' within rasterizer implementations, it does not make a general claim about 'most methods' relying on GPU rasterization for performance or enabling real-time interactivity. Source [S2] discusses performance comparisons between different composition methods (splat-every-sample vs. slice-by-slice) but does not support the generalization that most methods rely on GPU rasterization pipelines. The claim is a broad generalization not fully substantiated by the specific evidence provided in the sources.

It is distinguished from ray-casting methods by compositing along sheets (all pixels for a set of voxels simultaneously) rather than along rays, and from order-independent transparency (OIT) methods by relying on explicit depth sorting to enable hardware-accelerated rasterization [S1][S2, unofficial].

The claim states that the method is distinguished from ray-casting by compositing along sheets and from OIT by relying on explicit depth sorting to enable hardware-accelerated rasterization. Source [S1] supports the part about explicit depth sorting and hardware-accelerated rasterization (mentioning GPU blending hardware and sorting). However, Source [S2] actually contrasts 'splat-every-sample' composition with 'slice-by-slice (sheet buffer)' splatting, implying that the standard method described in [S1] (which uses sorting and alpha blending) is NOT the 'sheet buffer' method mentioned in [S2]. In fact, [S2] suggests that 'splat-every-sample' (which aligns more with the sorting/compositing described in [S1]) is distinct from the 'slice-by-slice' method. Therefore, the claim that the method is distinguished *by* compositing along sheets is contradicted or at least not supported by the provided texts, which present sheet-based splatting as a different, alternative approach to the sorting-based method.
supported
